title: Hash tables: hash functions, collisions and collision resolution
learningObjectives: Explain how a hash function maps a key to a table index and why distinct keys can produce the same index.
Distinguish separate chaining from open addressing, including the storage and search trade-offs of each.
Implement a separate-chaining table with linked bucket entries, key comparison, insertion, lookup and deletion.
Implement linear probing with explicit EMPTY, OCCUPIED and DELETED states, and explain why deletion needs a tombstone.
Calculate load factor, describe clustering and resizing, and explain why changing capacity requires rehashing entries.
Test collisions, duplicate keys, absent keys, deletion, full tables, zero capacity and allocation failure while preserving memory ownership.

understand.concept: A hash table stores key-value entries in an array of buckets. A hash function converts a key into a hash value, and the table maps that value to a valid bucket index, commonly with a remainder operation. Different keys can map to the same bucket; this is a collision, not necessarily a defect. A collision-resolution strategy is therefore part of the data structure. Separate chaining keeps a collection of entries at each bucket, often as a linked list. Open addressing keeps entries in the bucket array itself and probes other positions when the preferred slot is occupied.
understand.whyItMatters: Hash tables can provide expected constant-time lookup, insertion and deletion when the hash function distributes keys well and the load factor is controlled. They are used in symbol tables, caches, indexes and dictionaries. Their performance and correctness depend on more than calculating an index: keys must be compared for equality, collisions must be resolved, capacity must be managed and memory must have clear ownership.
understand.analogy: Imagine a library assigning each book to a shelf section using a code derived from its catalogue number. Two books may be assigned to the same section. The librarian still checks each book's actual catalogue number instead of assuming that sharing a section makes them the same book.
understand.analogyLimit: A hash is not a unique identity and a bucket is not proof of key equality. Real hash tables also need defined behaviour for duplicates, deletion, capacity exhaustion, resizing and adversarial or poorly distributed keys.

keyTerms.definition: A deterministic function that maps a key to a hash value; equal keys must produce equal hash values.
A table position or collection associated with a hash result.
Two distinct keys map to the same bucket index.
Each bucket refers to a collection of entries, commonly a linked list.
All entries are stored in the array; a probe sequence searches for another slot after a collision.
The number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets or slots, depending on the design.
A deleted marker in open addressing that tells a search to continue probing rather than stop.
Recomputing table positions for all entries after capacity or hash configuration changes.

understand.history: Hashing grew from ideas in information retrieval and fast table lookup. Modern hash tables combine a hash function with collision-resolution and capacity policies. The term hash suggests transforming or mixing a key into a value used to locate its storage position; the result is an index aid, not a substitute for checking the original key.

explain.narrative:
For a table with capacity m, a simple integer-key example is `index = key % m`. The capacity must be nonzero before using the remainder operation. A simple remainder hash is useful for teaching but may distribute patterned keys poorly; production designs select a hash function appropriate to the key type and threat model.

In separate chaining, each bucket points to the first entry in a linked list. Insertion must compare keys and decide what a duplicate means. This lesson uses map-style behaviour: inserting an existing key updates its value. Lookup walks one chain and compares the complete key. Deletion unlinks the matching entry before freeing it. The table owns every allocated entry and must release all entries during destruction. With a reasonable distribution, expected chain length is related to the load factor n/m; worst-case operations can still be O(n).

In open addressing, a collision triggers a probe sequence. Linear probing checks `(start + step) % capacity` until it finds the key or a slot that proves the key is absent. A deleted slot cannot simply become EMPTY: a later key may have been placed beyond it during an earlier probe. Marking it DELETED (a tombstone) lets searches continue while allowing future insertions to reuse that slot. If every slot is occupied or deleted, insertion must report that no slot is available. Linear probing can cause primary clustering, where groups of occupied slots grow and attract more probes.

Load factor helps determine when a table should grow. When capacity changes, old bucket indices are generally no longer valid, so entries must be reinserted using the new capacity; copying the old array positions is not sufficient. The two examples use a fixed capacity to keep the core collision rules visible. A production implementation should define resizing, overflow limits, key ownership, hash quality and failure behaviour explicitly.

examples.title: Separate chaining with insertion, lookup, deletion and cleanup
examples.explanation: The table has seven bucket heads. bucket_index maps each unsigned key to a position from zero through six. Keys 10, 17 and 24 all map to bucket 3, so this run deliberately creates a collision chain. table_put first searches that chain; an existing key has its value updated, while a new key gets one allocated entry inserted at the front. Allocation is checked before the node is linked into the table. table_get compares the full key rather than trusting the bucket index. table_remove uses a pointer to the link that owns the current entry, unlinks the match and only then frees it. table_destroy walks every bucket, saves each next pointer before freeing the current entry, clears bucket heads and resets the size. The expected output reports value 170, then that key 17 is absent, with two entries remaining. The table owns its entries; callers must not retain or use entry pointers after removal or destruction.

examples.title: Open addressing with linear probing and tombstones
examples.explanation: Every slot has an explicit state. EMPTY means a search may stop because no earlier insertion could have passed this point in the probe sequence. OCCUPIED stores a key and value. DELETED is a tombstone: a search must continue beyond it because a colliding key may be stored later. table_put remembers the first tombstone but continues probing to ensure it does not create a duplicate key farther along the sequence. It inserts at the remembered tombstone when it reaches an EMPTY slot, or uses the tombstone after a full scan. table_get stops at EMPTY, skips DELETED and compares keys in OCCUPIED slots. table_remove marks the slot DELETED instead of EMPTY, preserving the search path for keys inserted later in the same cluster. Keys 10, 17 and 24 collide at the initial index; after removing 17, lookup for 24 still succeeds. Key 31 can reuse the tombstone. The table is fixed-size and reports failure when no reusable slot exists. A production table should also define resizing and a policy for cleaning up accumulated tombstones.

practise.guidedTask: Use capacity 7 and the integer hash function key % 7. Insert keys 10, 17, 24 and 31. Draw the separate-chaining bucket and the linear-probing slots after each insertion. Remove 17 and trace a lookup for 24 in both designs. Explain why a tombstone is needed for open addressing but a linked-chain deletion can unlink and free its node.
practise.independentTask: Extend one implementation with a documented duplicate-key policy and a resize operation. For separate chaining, allocate a larger bucket array and relink or reinsert every entry using the new capacity, handling allocation failure without losing the old table. For open addressing, rebuild into a larger empty array and remove tombstones. Test duplicate updates, several keys with the same initial index, missing keys, deletion at the start and middle of a probe sequence, a completely full table, and cleanup after a failed resize. Record the load factor before and after resizing.
hints: A hash function chooses where to begin; always compare the original key to confirm a match.
Use a nonzero capacity before applying the remainder operator to calculate an array index.
Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket collection; open addressing probes other array slots.
In linear probing, stop a search at EMPTY, but continue through DELETED tombstones.
When inserting, continue past a tombstone long enough to check that the same key is not already stored later in the probe sequence.
Changing capacity changes bucket positions. Rehash every entry, and define what happens if allocating the new table fails.

questions.prompt: Two different keys produce the same bucket index. What is this situation called?
options: A collision
A duplicate key by definition
A memory leak
A resize
questions.explanation: A collision occurs when distinct keys map to the same bucket. The table must resolve it and still compare the original keys.

questions.prompt: How does separate chaining commonly handle collisions?
options: It stores multiple entries in a collection at the bucket, often a linked list.
It overwrites the old key without comparing it.
It stops accepting all further keys.
It converts every key to a string.
questions.answer: It stores multiple entries in a collection at the bucket, often a linked list.
questions.explanation: Each bucket points to a chain or other collection of entries that share the same bucket index.

questions.prompt: Why should an open-addressing deletion usually leave a DELETED tombstone instead of changing the slot to EMPTY?
options: A search must be able to continue to colliding keys stored later in the probe sequence.
It makes the key larger.
It automatically resizes the table.
It prevents all future collisions.
questions.answer: A search must be able to continue to colliding keys stored later in the probe sequence.
questions.explanation: Changing the slot to EMPTY could make a later key appear absent because a lookup would stop too early.

questions.prompt: What does the load factor n/m represent in a table with n entries and m buckets or slots?
options: The ratio of stored entries to table capacity
The number of collisions multiplied by the key size
The byte size of one entry
The number of deleted nodes only
questions.answer: The ratio of stored entries to table capacity
questions.explanation: Load factor describes how full the table is and helps guide resizing policies.

questions.prompt: After increasing a hash table's capacity, why must entries normally be rehashed?
options: The bucket index depends on capacity, so old positions may no longer be correct.
The keys become invalid C objects.
The hash function must return unique values.
The table no longer needs key comparisons.
questions.answer: The bucket index depends on capacity, so old positions may no longer be correct.
questions.explanation: A changed capacity changes the mapping from hash values to indices. Reinsert entries using the new capacity and collision policy.
